title: Non-Invasive Quantification of Blood Chemistry Profiles from Standard Electrocardiogram Signals
content:
Electrocardiographic (ECG) monitoring is a cornerstone of inpatient surveillance, yet bedside telemetry rarely exploits the full informational content of the signal. Emerging evidence that systemic biological variables can be inferred from raw ECG waveforms suggests that continuous ECG could serve as a non-invasive surrogate for laboratory monitoring. We developed and validated an end-to-end machine-learning framework to infer abnormalities in key blood parameters directly from standard ECG recordings.
Using MIMIC-IV ECG traces paired with laboratory measurements acquired within 30 minutes, we trained two convolutional neural network architectures to classify 55 parameter/threshold combinations across 29 routinely measured laboratory parameters into normal and abnormal ranges, using 12-lead and single-lead (II) inputs combined with age and gender. Data were temporally split by subject to mimic prospective validation. The best models were further evaluated on long-term ICU ECG traces from MIMIC-III-WDB. Performance was assessed via ROC-AUC, average precision, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and F1-score with bootstrap 95% CIs.
The final datasets comprised 266,896 samples from 104,664 subjects (MIMIC-IV) and 79,855 samples from 5,292 subjects (MIMIC-III). In the 12-lead setting, 20 of 55 combinations achieved a lower ROC-AUC 95% CI bound above 0.7; hypokalemia (potassium < 3.3 mEq/L) performed best (ROC-AUC 0.834 [0.817–0.849]). Single-lead performance decreased only slightly, whereas generalization to ICU single-lead recordings declined. Saliency analysis revealed physiologically plausible focus, notably on the T-wave for hypokalemia.
Standard ECGs contain exploitable signatures of systemic biochemical alteration, enabling classification of multiple laboratory abnormalities with moderate-to-good discrimination. Precision limitations caution against interruptive alerting for rare endpoints, but ECG-based estimation holds promise as a non-invasive screening and triage tool in acute care.
